answer_text:
Let \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) be an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{Q}\). A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-field homomorphism
\[
\sigma:\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathbb{C}
\]
fixing \(\mathbb{Q}\) is automatically injective, so we are counting \(\mathbb{Q}\)-embeddings of \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) into \(\mathbb{C}\).

### 1. Upper bound

The field \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) is countable. Therefore any such homomorphism is determined by its values on a countable set of elements, each of which lies in \(\mathbb{C}\). Hence the number of possible homomorphisms is at most

\[
|\mathbb{C}|^{\aleph_0}
=
(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}
=
2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

So there are at most \(2^{\aleph_0}\) such homomorphisms.

### 2. Lower bound

Let \(P\) be the set of rational primes, and define

\[
K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p}:p\in P)\subseteq \mathbb{C}.
\]

For each function

\[
\varepsilon:P\to\{\pm 1\},
\]

there is a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-embedding \(K\to\mathbb{C}\) sending

\[
\sqrt{p}\mapsto \varepsilon(p)\sqrt{p}
\qquad\text{for every prime }p.
\]

Indeed, on every finite subfield \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_n})\), the distinct primes give independent square classes modulo \(\mathbb{Q}^{\times 2}\), so the sign choices define a field automorphism. These finite automorphisms are compatible, giving a well-defined embedding of \(K\).

There are

\[
2^{|P|}=2^{\aleph_0}
\]

such sign choices, and they give distinct embeddings of \(K\) into \(\mathbb{C}\).

Now \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) is algebraic over \(K\), and \(\mathbb{C}\) is algebraically closed. By the standard extension theorem for algebraic extensions, every embedding \(K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}\) extends to a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-embedding

\[
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}.
\]

Thus there are at least \(2^{\aleph_0}\) such homomorphisms.

Combining the upper and lower bounds, the number of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-field homomorphisms is exactly

\[
\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}.
\]

Equivalently, there are continuum many such homomorphisms.
